\oldpage{41}
The global theory of ideals of analytic functions, due to K. Oka [@10] and H. Cartan [@2; @3; @4], holds not only for domains of holomorphy but also for a larger class of complex analytic manifolds introduced by K. Stein [@11], and which notably contains all the smooth analytic submanifolds, of arbitrary dimension $p$, of the complex space of arbitrary dimension $n>p$.

The fundamental theorems of this theory are nicely expressed in the language of cohomology, which suggests generalisations and provides a useful tool when it comes to using the results.
In this conference, we will first give an exposition on the fundamental ideas: that of a *sheaf*, and that of *cohomology* with coefficients in a sheaf.
We will then state the fundamental theorems.
Finally, we will give some applications to global problems concerning Stein manifolds;
other applications will be given in the conference by J.-P. Serre.

# Sheaves on a topological space[^1] {#section-1}

[^1]: The notion of *sheaf* was introduced by J. Leray in the study of homological properties of a continuous map. See J. Leray, *Journ. de Math. pures et appliquées* **29**, 1950, pp. 1--139; it is in this work that we find (at the bottom of page 75) a definition of cohomology with coefficients in a sheaf, limited, in truth, to the case of a locally compact space $X$ (and it deals with "compactly supported" cohomology). The definition of sheaves adopted here is a bit different; it is due to Lazard and was explained in [@5], where the theory of cohomology with coefficients in a sheaf was developed (exposés XIV to XX).

Let $X$ be a topological space.
A *sheaf of abelian groups* on $X$, or simply a *sheaf*, is defined by the data:
\oldpage{42}

1. of a function $x\mapsto\sh{F}_x$ that, to each point $x\in X$, associates an abelian group $\sh{F}_x$ (which we denote additively);
2. of a (not necessarily separated) topology on the union $\sh{F}$ of the sets $\sh{F}_x$.

Before giving the axioms that these data must satisfy, we denote by $p$ the map from $\sh{F}$ to $X$ that, to each $\alpha\in\sh{F}$, associates the point $x$ such that $\alpha\in\sh{F}_x$.
We impose two axioms:

::: {.rmenv title="F₁" latex="{F\textsubscript{I}}"}
The map $\alpha\mapsto-\alpha$ that, to each $\alpha\in\sh{F}$ associates the inverse of $\alpha$ in the group $\sh{F}_{p\alpha}$, is a continuous map from $\sh{F}$ to $\sh{F}$.
The map $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha+\beta$ defined on the set $\sh{G}$ of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ such that $p(\alpha)=p(\beta)$, and that sends such a pair to the sum $\alpha+\beta$ in the group $\sh{F}_{p(\alpha)}$, is a continuous map from the subset $\sh{G}$ of $\sh{F}\times\sh{F}$ to $\sh{F}$.
:::

::: {.rmenv title="F₂" latex="{F\textsubscript{II}}"}
The map $p$ is a *local homeomorphism*, i.e. every element $\alpha\in\sh{F}$ admits an open neighbourhood $V$ such that the restriction of $p$ to $V$ is a homeomorphism from $V$ to an open subset of $X$.
:::

If $U$ is a subset of $X$, then the collection of the $\sh{F}_x$ for $x\in U$, endowed with the topology induced by that of $\sh{F}$, is evidently a sheaf on $U$;
we denote it by $\sh{F}(U)$, and we call it the sheaf *induced* by $\sh{F}$ on $U$.

::: {.itenv title="Example" latex="{Example}"}
Let $G$ be an abelian group.
Let $\sh{F}$ be the product $G\times X$, endowed with the product topology (with $G$ being endowed with the discrete topology).
The subset $\sh{F}_x$ of pairs $(g,x)$, where $g$ runs over $G$, is evidently endowed with the structure of an abelian group (isomorphic to $G$).
We can immediately verify the axioms (F~I~) and (F~II~).
This sheaf is called the *constant sheaf* defined by $G$, and is also denoted by $G$.
:::

Let $\sh{F}$ be an arbitrary sheaf on $X$.
We define a *section* of $\sh{F}$ over an open $U\subset X$ to be a *continuous* map $s\colon U\to\sh{F}$ such that $p\circ s$ is the identity;
$s$ is then a homeomorphism from $U$ to its image $s(U)$.
Axiom (F~II~) implies the following: if two sections are equal at a point $x\in U$, then they are equal at all points in a neighbourhood of $x$.
The map $s$ that, to each $x\in U$, associates the identity element $0_x\in\sh{F}_x$, is a section (by (F~I~));
we call it the *zero section*.
The set $\Gamma(U,\sh{F})$ of sections of $\sh{F}$ over $U$ is endowed with the structure of an abelian group, thanks to (F~I~), and the zero section is the identity element of this group.

If $U$ and $V$ are opens such that $V\subset U$, then every section over $U$ induces a section over $V$.
The group $\sh{F}_x$ is the inductive limit of the groups $\Gamma(U,\sh{F})$ taken over open neighbourhoods $U$ of $x$.

\oldpage{43}
In practice, a sheaf on $X$ is often defined in the following way: we give abelian groups $\sh{F}_U$ attached to certain opens $U\subset X$ that form a fundamental system of opens of the topology of $X$; and, for every pair $(U,V)$ such that $V\subset U$, we give a homomorphism $f_{VU}\colon\sh{F}_U\to\sh{F}_V$, such that, for $W\subset V\subset U$, we have that $f_{WU}=f_{WV}\circ f_{VU}$.
We then take $\sh{F}_x$ to be the inductive limit of the $\sh{F}_U$ over the opens $U$ that contain $x$; and, on the union $\sh{F}$ of the $\sh{F}_x$, we define the topology $\scr{T}$ as follows: for every open $U$ and every $\alpha\in\sh{F}_U$, let $[\alpha]$ be the set of images of $\alpha$ in the $\sh{F}_x$ associated to the points $x\in U$; by definition, the subsets $[\alpha]$ of $\sh{F}$ constitute a fundamental system of opens of the topology $\scr{T}$.
Axioms (F~I~) and (F~II~) are satisfied.
We have an obvious homomorphism $\sh{F}_U\to\Gamma(U,\sh{F})$, but this is not necessarily an isomorphism
Indeed, two different methods of definition can lead to defining the same sheaf.
For the homomorphism $\sh{F}_U\to\Gamma(U,\sh{F})$ to be an *isomorphism*, it is necessary and sufficient that, for every system of opens $U_i$ with union $U$, and every system of elements $\alpha_i\in\sh{F}_{U_i}$ such that $\alpha_i$ and $\alpha_j$ have the same image in $\sh{F}_{U_i\cap U_j}$, there exist a unique $\alpha\in\sh{F}_U$ such that $F_{U_iU}(\alpha)=\alpha_i$ for all $i$.

::: {.rmenv title="Example" latex="{Example}"}
Let $\sh{F}_U$ be the additive group of real-valued (resp. complex-valued) functions defined and continuous on $U$.
If $V\subset U$, then the homomorphism $\sh{F}_U\to\sh{F}_V$ will be that which sends a function defined on $U$ to its restriction to $V$.
Then $\sh{F}_x$ is the additive group of *germs of continuous functions* at the point $x$;
and $\sh{F}$ is called the sheaf of germs of real (resp. complex) continuous functions; $\sh{F}_U$ is isomorphism to the group of sections of $\sh{F}$ over $U$.
:::

::: {.rmenv title="Remark" latex="{Remark}"}
We have defined sheaves of abelian groups, but it is clear that analogous definitions can be given for any algebraic structure.
:::


# Subsheaf, homomorphism, quotient sheaf {#section-2}

Let $\sh{F}$ be a sheaf on $X$.
